title: Empirical Asset Pricing with Polars
text:
Preface
A reader’s companion in Python Polars to Empirical Asset Pricing: The Cross Section of Stock Returns by Bali, Engle, and Murray (2016). We refer to the authors as BEM. The methods chapters use their 1988–2012 annual teaching sample. The empirical chapters reconstruct the CRSP sample, estimate market beta, and examine the size effect and value premium using legacy CRSP. See the eap_pl function reference for the shared Polars helpers. Render with your own copies of the WRDS data.
See 1  Preliminaries for the inputs and WRDS tables for their source update dates.





Bali, Turan G., Robert F. Engle, and Scott Murray. 2016. Empirical Asset Pricing: The Cross Section of Stock Returns. John Wiley & Sons. https://www.wiley.com/en-us/empirical-asset-pricing-the-cross-section-of-stock-returns-p-9781118095041.

title: 1  Preliminaries
text:
1.1 Sample
Chapter 2 uses the annual teaching sample of Bali et al. (2016), covering U.S. common stocks at each year-end from 1988 through 2012. The empirical replications use longer monthly samples.
The examples read local Parquet files through era_pl.load_parquet(). The DATA_DIR setting points to the data root, and each table lives at DATA_DIR/schema/table.parquet. You can create these files from WRDS with the setup script in Section 1.1.2.

1.1.2 Create the Parquet repository
Copy .env.example to .env in the book checkout and set DATA_DIR to your Parquet root and WRDS_ID to your WRDS username. After uv sync, run the setup script from that checkout. If you already have the source files there, you can skip this step. If your WRDS account lacks access to the legacy CRSP tables, use licensed SIZ extracts at the corresponding paths.
uv run scripts/download_wrds_tables.py
The following Python example shows how the script uses db2pq.wrds_update_pq() to export the WRDS tables to DATA_DIR.
from db2pq import wrds_update_pq
from dotenv import load_dotenv

load_dotenv()

tables = {
    "crsp": ["msf", "dsf", "msenames", "msedelist", "msi", "ccmxpf_lnkused"],
    "comp": ["funda"],
    "ff": ["factors_monthly", "factors_daily"],
}

for schema, names in tables.items():
    for name in names:
        wrds_update_pq(name, schema)


1.1.3 Other inputs
The annual methods chapters construct December betas, size, and book-to-market from the local source data when needed. See Chapters 8, 9, and 10 for how each measure is constructed. The monthly Size and Value analyses read the 12-month daily beta from eap.betas, which the Beta chapter can export during the full render. See the render instructions.
The size builder and the CRSP and Value chapters use the BLS all-items CPI for urban consumers, not seasonally adjusted, from FRED, to express market capitalizations in December 2012 dollars. This file does not come from WRDS.
Chapter 13 uses the December 2013 Pástor–Stambaugh liquidity release bundled with eap_pl.
For comparisons across Fama–French vintages, see eap_pl.get_ff_factors(). The loader checks the archive’s checksum and keeps a local copy for later renders. Chapter 14 and Chapter 15 use the June 2014 archive. The four-factor volatility model also uses its daily momentum factor.

title: 1  Preliminaries
text:
1.2 Winsorization and Truncation
Winsorization caps values outside chosen percentile cutoffs at the corresponding cutoff. Truncation sets those values to missing, so analyses that require the variable exclude those observations. In Section 1.2, Bali et al. (2016) describe both methods as ways to limit the influence of extreme values. They suggest capping observations that still convey information about genuinely high or low values, and consider truncation when the extremes appear to come from a different process. They urge caution when the conclusions depend on which treatment is used.
BEM compute the cutoffs separately for each year or month because they analyze each period’s cross-section before summarizing the results over time. Their 0.5% rule uses the 0.5th and 99.5th percentiles. In Chapter 3, both variables are winsorized for Pearson correlations, and Spearman correlations use ranks of the original values. In Chapter 6, the regressors are winsorized and the excess-return outcome is used as observed.
We compute the winsorization cutoffs by linear interpolation with .era.winsorize(prob=0.005, quantile_method="linear"). The eap_pl.winsorized_corr() helper applies this rule to each variable after keeping pairs with two finite values. In Chapter 8, .over("month") computes cutoffs separately for each month’s beta estimates. We then fit the Fama–MacBeth regressions with statspai.fama_macbeth().
For examples using .era.winsorize() and .era.truncate() and a comparison with robust regression, see Chapter 24 of Empirical Research in Accounting.

title: 1  Preliminaries
text:
1.3 Newey and West (1987) Adjustment
In Section 1.3, Bali et al. (2016) explain why inference on a time-series mean can be sensitive to changing variance and correlation across periods. Regressing a series on a constant gives its sample mean as the intercept. The adjustment of Newey and West (1987) estimates the standard error using covariances across periods, with less weight on more distant lags. Depending on the pattern of autocorrelation, the adjustment can increase or decrease the standard error. In Chapter 5, BEM use the adjustment for average portfolio returns and spreads, and in time-series factor regressions for portfolio alphas.
For Fama–MacBeth regressions, BEM apply the adjustment to the sequence of estimated coefficients, with one estimate per cross-section. BEM motivate six lags with a rule of thumb for a series of about 600 monthly observations and also use six lags in their annual example, which has only 24 coefficient estimates. Gow et al. (2010) call this procedure FM-NW and find that its standard errors can remain too small when the underlying panel has both cross-sectional and time-series dependence. A short coefficient series provides limited information about persistence in the underlying data (Gow et al. 2010, 488).
The annual, beta, size, and book-to-market regressions replicated here use realized excess returns over nonoverlapping holding periods. This resembles the return-based application in Gow et al. (2010, sec. V), where shared shocks across stocks are the main concern. For slope inference, the relevant serial dependence involves the joint behavior of regressors and residuals. Size is highly persistent in our replications. Across specifications, the pooled lag-one correlations between residuals for the same stock range from about \(-0.05\) to \(-0.01\).
For every slope in the monthly replications, the ordinary and six-lag tests agree at the 5% level. Section 6.2 shows how the adjustment changes inference on size in the annual example.
For more on Newey–West, Fama–MacBeth, and clustering, see Section 5.6 of Empirical Research in Accounting in the StatsPAI edition or the Polars edition.

title: 2  Summary Statistics
text:
2.1 Implementation
In Chapter 2, Bali et al. (2016) summarize the distribution of stock characteristics within each year, then average those statistics across years. This gives each year’s cross-section equal weight.

title: 2  Summary Statistics
text:
2.1.1 Periodic Cross-Sectional Summary Statistics
The sample covers U.S. common stocks at each December 31 from 1988 through 2012. We take the December value of the 12-month daily beta from Chapter 8. It uses all available daily excess returns in the calendar year and requires at least 200 matched observations.

import polars as pl

from eap_pl import build_annual_panel, load_annual_betas

annual_beta = load_annual_betas().collect()

For each year, compute the statistics across the stocks with a beta. We use the sample standard deviation, bias-adjusted skewness and excess kurtosis, and linearly interpolated percentiles. The count is the number of available values in that cross-section.

def cross_section(variable):
    x = pl.col(variable)
    return [
        x.mean().alias("Mean"),
        x.std().alias("SD"),
        x.skew(bias=False).alias("Skew"),
        x.kurtosis(fisher=True, bias=False).alias("Kurt."),
        x.min().alias("Min"),
        x.quantile(.05, interpolation="linear").alias("5%"),
        x.quantile(.25, interpolation="linear").alias("25%"),
        x.median().alias("Median"),
        x.quantile(.75, interpolation="linear").alias("75%"),
        x.quantile(.95, interpolation="linear").alias("95%"),
        x.max().alias("Max"),
        x.count().alias("n"),
    ]

annual_stats = (
    annual_beta.group_by("year")
    .agg(cross_section("Beta"))
    .sort("year")
)

To describe the typical cross-section, take the mean of each column in Table 2.1. For example, if \(n_t\) stocks have valid betas in year \(t\), their mean is \(\bar{\beta}_t = \sum_{i=1}^{n_t}\widehat{\beta}_{i,t}/n_t\). The table reports \(T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\bar{\beta}_t\). A pooled mean would instead give years with more observations more weight. The same two-step procedure applies to the median and other statistics.

title: 2  Summary Statistics
text:
2.2 Presentation and Interpretation
We also summarize year-end market capitalization in millions of dollars, its natural logarithm (size), book-to-market, and the following calendar year’s excess return. build_annual_panel() assembles these observations using start_year and end_year, which default to 1988 and 2012.
The December beta observations already calculated for Table 2.1 define the stock-years in the panel. The helper uses permno and formation year as the join keys. build_sizes() provides December market capitalization and its log, as described in Chapter 9. build_book_to_market() supplies the ratio of prior-year fiscal book equity to prior December market capitalization, as described in Chapter 10. We use its signed ratio, consistent with the negative observations in BEM Table 2.3.
betas = annual_betas.lazy().filter(pl.col("year").is_between(start_year, end_year))
keys = ["permno", "year"]
sizes = build_sizes()
capitalizations = (
    sizes.lazy()
    .filter(pl.col("month").dt.month() == 12)
    .select("permno", year=pl.col("month").dt.year(), MktCap="cap", Size="log_cap")
    .filter(pl.col("year").is_between(start_year, end_year))
)
book_to_market = (
    build_book_to_market(sizes).lazy()
    .filter(pl.col("month").dt.month() == 12)
    .select("permno", year=pl.col("month").dt.year(), BM="bm_raw")
    .filter(pl.col("year").is_between(start_year, end_year))
)
For each stock and holding year, the helper compounds the available monthly returns reported by CRSP. BEM §1.1 does not spell out how its annual returns handle delistings. The helper compounds the monthly risk-free returns separately, requiring 12 observations for the year.
stock_returns = (
    load_parquet("msf", "crsp")
    .filter(
        pl.col("date").is_between(pl.date(start_year + 1, 1, 1), pl.date(end_year, 12, 31)),
        pl.col("ret").is_finite(),
    )
    .with_columns(year=pl.col("date").dt.year())
    .group_by(keys)
    .agg(gross_stock=(1 + pl.col("ret")).product())
)
risk_free = (
    load_parquet("factors_monthly", "ff")
    .with_columns(year=pl.col("date").dt.year())
    .filter(pl.col("year").is_between(start_year + 1, end_year))
    .group_by("year")
    .agg(gross_rf=(1 + pl.col("rf")).product(), n=pl.col("rf").count())
    .filter(pl.col("n") == 12)
)
Subtract the annual risk-free return from the stock return and express the difference in percentage points. Subtracting one from the holding year aligns the return with the characteristics measured the preceding December. For example, the return earned in 1989 is joined to the stock’s 1988 characteristics.
next_year = (
    stock_returns.join(risk_free, on="year", validate="m:1")
    .select(
        "permno",
        year=pl.col("year") - 1,
        excess=100 * (pl.col("gross_stock") - pl.col("gross_rf")),
    )
)
The left joins keep each stock-year in the beta sample even when a characteristic or return is missing. end_year is both the last formation year and the last calendar year included in the return calculations. In the default sample, this leaves the 2012 formation rows with missing next-year returns. The final .collect() returns the assembled panel as a Polars DataFrame.
return (
    betas.join(capitalizations, on=keys, how="left", validate="1:1")
    .join(book_to_market, on=keys, how="left", validate="1:1")
    .join(next_year, on=keys, how="left", validate="1:1")
    .collect()
)

annual_panel = build_annual_panel(annual_betas=annual_beta)

Apply the same summary to each variable separately. This keeps stocks with a beta but no book-to-market ratio in the beta row. The observation count reflects the available data for each variable.

variables = ["Beta", "MktCap", "Size", "BM", "excess"]
all_stats = (
    annual_panel.unpivot(on=variables, index="year", variable_name="Measure")
    .group_by("year", "Measure")
    .agg(cross_section("value"))
    .group_by("Measure")
    .agg(pl.exclude("year", "Measure").mean())
)

title: 3  Correlation
text:
3.1 Implementation
In Chapter 3, Bali et al. (2016) compare the cross-sectional associations among beta, size, book-to-market, and next-year excess return. We use the 1988–2012 annual panel from Chapter 2.

title: 3  Correlation
text:
3.1.1 Periodic Cross-Sectional Correlations
For variables \(X\) and \(Y\) in year \(t\), keep the \(n_t\) stocks for which both variables are observed. The Pearson correlation measures linear association. With \(\bar X_t\) and \(\bar Y_t\) denoting the means in this paired cross-section, the correlation is
\[
\rho_t(X,Y)=
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n_t}(X_{i,t}-\bar X_t)(Y_{i,t}-\bar Y_t)}
{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n_t}(X_{i,t}-\bar X_t)^2}
\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n_t}(Y_{i,t}-\bar Y_t)^2}}.
\tag{3.1}\]
For the Pearson entries in Table 3.1, winsorize each variable at the 0.5th and 99.5th percentiles of the paired cross-section before computing its mean and correlation.
The Spearman correlation measures association between ranks. Let \(x_{i,t}\) and \(y_{i,t}\) be the ranks of the original values within the paired cross-section, with rank 1 assigned to the smallest value. When neither variable has ties, the rank difference \(d_{i,t}=x_{i,t}-y_{i,t}\) gives
\[
\rho_t^S(X,Y)=1-\frac{6\sum_{i=1}^{n_t}d_{i,t}^2}{n_t(n_t^2-1)}.
\tag{3.2}\]
With ties, give equal values their average rank and compute the Pearson correlation of the two rank vectors. This is the calculation used by pl.corr(method="spearman"), including when Equation 3.2 applies.

from eap_pl import correlation_matrix, period_correlations

variables = {"Beta": "Beta", "Size": "Size", "BM": "Book-to-market", "excess": "Next-year return"}
annual = period_correlations(annual_panel, variables, "year").sort("year")

\tag{3.4}\]

3.2 Interpreting Correlations
The two companion figures plot the annual coefficients in Table 3.1. Each panel uses formation years on the horizontal axis. In the second figure, the return paired with year \(t\) comes from year \(t+1\).

from plotnine_polars import aes

def plot_correlations(pairs):
    labels = [f"{variables[a]} and {variables[b]}" for a, b in pairs]
    correlations = pl.concat(
        annual.select("year", Pearson=f"Pearson {a}–{b}", Spearman=f"Spearman {a}–{b}")
        .unpivot(index="year", variable_name="method", value_name="correlation")
        .with_columns(pair=pl.lit(label))
        for (a, b), label in zip(pairs, labels, strict=True)
    ).with_columns(pl.col("pair").cast(pl.Enum(labels)))
    return (
        correlations
        .ggplot(aes(x="year", y="correlation", color="method", linetype="method"))
        .geom_hline(yintercept=0, color="#b3b3b3", size=0.4)
        .geom_line(na_rm=True)
        .facet_wrap("pair", ncol=1)
        .scale_x_continuous(breaks=range(1988, 2013, 4))
        .scale_color_manual(values={"Pearson": "#24639a", "Spearman": "#ac4c27"})
        .scale_linetype_manual(values={"Pearson": "solid", "Spearman": "dashed"})
        .labs(x="Formation year", y="Correlation", color="", linetype="")
        .theme_minimal()
        .add_theme(figure_size=(8, 6), legend_position="top")
    )

title: 4  Persistence Analysis
text:
4.1 Implementation
In Chapter 4, Bali et al. (2016) measure persistence by correlating a stock characteristic with its own future value across stocks. We use the December 1988–2012 panel from Chapter 2, including its signed book-to-market ratio.

title: 4  Persistence Analysis
text:
4.1.1 Periodic Cross-Sectional Persistence
For a lag of \(\tau\) years, match stocks by permno in years \(t\) and \(t+\tau\). For each characteristic \(X\), keep the set \(\mathcal S_{t,\tau}\) of stocks with finite values of \(X\) in both years. Within this matched sample, winsorize each year’s values separately at the 0.5th and 99.5th percentiles. Using the winsorized values and their cross-sectional means, the Pearson correlation is
\[
\rho_{t,t+\tau}(X)=
\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i\in\mathcal S_{t,\tau}}
      (X_{i,t}-\bar X_t)(X_{i,t+\tau}-\bar X_{t+\tau})}
     {\displaystyle\sqrt{\sum_{i\in\mathcal S_{t,\tau}}(X_{i,t}-\bar X_t)^2}
                   \sqrt{\sum_{i\in\mathcal S_{t,\tau}}(X_{i,t+\tau}-\bar X_{t+\tau})^2}}.
\tag{4.1}\]
Shift the future year’s join key back by the lag so that each stock’s observation in \(t+\tau\) joins its observation in \(t\). Use the same winsorized Pearson correlation as in Chapter 3.

from eap_pl import winsorized_corr

measures = ["Beta", "Size", "BM"]
lags = range(1, 6)
characteristics = annual_panel.select("permno", "year", *measures)

def annual_persistence(lag):
    future = characteristics.with_columns(year=pl.col("year") - lag)
    return (
        characteristics.join(future, on=["permno", "year"], suffix="_future", validate="1:1")
        .group_by("year")
        .agg(
            winsorized_corr(pl.col(x), pl.col(f"{x}_future")).fill_nan(None).alias(x)
            for x in measures
        )
        .with_columns(pl.lit(lag).alias("Lag"))
    )

annual = pl.concat([annual_persistence(lag) for lag in lags]).sort("Lag", "year")

title: 4  Persistence Analysis
text:
4.2 Interpreting Persistence
Low beta persistence can reflect changing market exposures, noisy estimates, or both. Overlapping estimation windows can raise the correlation because the two estimates use some of the same returns. Here the December 12-month betas use daily returns from separate calendar years. The set of stocks with valid measurements at both dates can also change with the lag, so differences across lags reflect both the time between measurements and the stocks observed at both dates.

title: 5  Portfolio Analysis
text:
5.1 Univariate Portfolio Analysis
In Chapter 5, Bali et al. (2016) use portfolio sorts to study how next year’s excess return varies with beta, market capitalization, and book-to-market. We form portfolios at each December year-end from 1988 to 2012 using the panel from Chapter 2. Holding returns run from 1989 to 2012.

title: 5  Portfolio Analysis
text:
5.1.1 Breakpoints
In year \(t\), let \(\{X_t\}\) be the available values of the sort variable and \(p_k\) the probability used for breakpoint \(k\). For \(n_P\) portfolios, calculate \(n_P-1\) breakpoints.
\[
B_{k,t}=\operatorname{Pctl}_{p_k}(\{X_t\}).
\tag{5.1}\]
The beta sort uses the 10th, 20th, 40th, 60th, 80th, and 90th percentiles. The first and last groups each hold about a tenth of the stocks, giving a closer look at both tails of the distribution. We use linear interpolation for the percentiles.

def breakpoints(stocks, variable, probabilities, by):
    return stocks.group_by(by).agg(
        pl.col(variable).quantile(p, interpolation="linear").alias(f"{p:.0%}")
        for p in probabilities
    )

seven_way = [.10, .20, .40, .60, .80, .90]

5.1.2 Portfolio Formation
With \(B_{0,t}=-\infty\) and \(B_{n_P,t}=\infty\), portfolio \(k\) contains
\[
P_{k,t}=\{i:B_{k-1,t}\le X_{i,t}\le B_{k,t}\}.
\tag{5.2}\]
Both endpoints are included, as in BEM. A stock exactly on a breakpoint can enter both adjacent portfolios. The code joins each stock to its year’s breakpoint intervals, then keeps the intervals that contain its sort value.

from itertools import pairwise

def form_portfolios(stocks, variable, breaks, by, label):
    cutoffs = [pl.col(column) for column in breaks.columns if column not in by]
    edges = [pl.lit(-float("inf")), *cutoffs, pl.lit(float("inf"))]
    intervals = pl.concat([
        breaks.select(*by, pl.lit(group).alias(label), lower=lower, upper=upper)
        for group, (lower, upper) in enumerate(pairwise(edges), 1)
    ])
    return (
        stocks.join(intervals, on=by)
        .filter(pl.col(variable).is_between("lower", "upper"))
        .drop("lower", "upper")
    )

5.1.3 Average Portfolio Values
For an available outcome \(Y\) and weight \(W\), the portfolio outcome is
\[
Y_{k,t}=\frac{\sum_{i\in P_{k,t}} W_{i,t}Y_{i,t}}
              {\sum_{i\in P_{k,t}} W_{i,t}}.
\tag{5.3}\]
Here \(Y_{i,t}\) is the stock’s excess return in year \(t+1\). For equal weights use \(W_{i,t}=1\). For value weights use December market capitalization and calculate the numerator and denominator on the same set of stocks with available returns and weights. For each year, form the high-minus-low spread
\[
Y_{\mathrm{Diff},t}=Y_{n_P,t}-Y_{1,t}.
\tag{5.4}\]

portfolio_columns = [str(group) for group in range(1, 8)]
univariate_columns = [*portfolio_columns, "7–1"]
last_holding_year = 2012

def univariate_series(cells, outcome):
    return (
        cells.pivot(on="portfolio", index="year", values=outcome)
        .sort("year")
        .select("year", *portfolio_columns, (pl.col("7") - pl.col("1")).alias("7–1"))
    )

r = pl.col("excess")
valid = pl.all_horizontal(r.is_finite(), pl.col("MktCap").is_finite())
w = pl.col("MktCap").filter(valid)
beta_returns = (

5.2 Bivariate Independent-Sort Analysis

5.2.1 Breakpoints
To study returns across market-cap groups while controlling for beta, keep stocks with both characteristics. For an independent sort, calculate both sets of breakpoints across this same cross-section. Let \(j\) index the \(n_1\) groups of \(X_1\) and \(k\) index the \(n_2\) groups of \(X_2\).
\[
B_{1j,t}=\operatorname{Pctl}_{p_{1j}}(\{X_{1t}\}).
\tag{5.10}\]
\[
B_{2k,t}=\operatorname{Pctl}_{p_{2k}}(\{X_{2t}\}).
\tag{5.11}\]
We use the 30th and 70th percentiles for beta and the 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles for market capitalization.
Use the same percentile and membership functions as in the univariate sort. The second set of breakpoints is grouped only by year here. The dependent sort uses the same pipeline with an additional grouping key for the first portfolio.

control_ports = ["1", "2", "3"]

def bivariate_sort(first, second, *, dependent=False):
    stocks = annual_panel.filter(pl.all_horizontal(pl.col(first, second).is_finite()))
    first_breaks = breakpoints(stocks, first, [.30, .70], ["year"])
    first_groups = form_portfolios(stocks, first, first_breaks, ["year"], "control")

    by = ["year", "control"] if dependent else ["year"]
    breakpoint_sample = first_groups if dependent else stocks
    second_breaks = breakpoints(breakpoint_sample, second, [.25, .50, .75], by)
    members = form_portfolios(first_groups, second, second_breaks, by, "target")
    return members, first_breaks, second_breaks

independent, first_breaks, second_breaks = bivariate_sort("Beta", "MktCap")

5.2.2 Portfolio Formation

Pivot the portfolio cells so that the beta groups are columns and the market-cap groups are rows within each year.

def control_grid(cells, value):
    return (
        cells.pivot(on="control", index=["year", "target"], values=value)
        .sort("year", "target")
        .select("year", "target", *control_ports)

5.2.3 Average Portfolio Values
Within each of the 12 portfolios, compute the outcome using the univariate weighting rule. The example uses equal weights.
\[
Y_{j,k,t}=\frac{\sum_{i\in P_{j,k,t}}W_{i,t}Y_{i,t}}
                {\sum_{i\in P_{j,k,t}}W_{i,t}}.
\tag{5.13}\]
A high-minus-low spread along market capitalization holds the beta group fixed. A spread along beta holds the market-cap group fixed.
\[
Y_{j,\mathrm{Diff},t}=Y_{j,n_2,t}-Y_{j,1,t}.
\tag{5.14}\]
\[
Y_{\mathrm{Diff},k,t}=Y_{n_1,k,t}-Y_{1,k,t}.
\tag{5.15}\]
We can also average across either set of portfolios. Each group receives equal weight, even when stock counts differ.
\[
Y_{\mathrm{Avg},k,t}=\frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{j=1}^{n_1}Y_{j,k,t}.
\tag{5.16}\]
\[
Y_{j,\mathrm{Avg},t}=\frac{1}{n_2}\sum_{k=1}^{n_2}Y_{j,k,t}.
\tag{5.17}\]
\[
Y_{\mathrm{Avg},\mathrm{Avg},t}
=\frac{1}{n_1}\sum_jY_{j,\mathrm{Avg},t}
=\frac{1}{n_2}\sum_kY_{\mathrm{Avg},k,t}
=\frac{1}{n_1n_2}\sum_j\sum_kY_{j,k,t}.
\tag{5.18}\]
The difference in differences compares the market-cap spread in the highest-beta group with the spread in the lowest-beta group. The same result comes from comparing beta spreads across market-cap groups.
\[
\begin{aligned}
Y_{\mathrm{Diff},\mathrm{Diff},t}
&=Y_{n_1,n_2,t}-Y_{n_1,1,t}-Y_{1,n_2,t}+Y_{1,1,t}\\
&=Y_{\mathrm{Diff},n_2,t}-Y_{\mathrm{Diff},1,t}\\
&=Y_{n_1,\mathrm{Diff},t}-Y_{1,\mathrm{Diff},t}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{5.19}\]

Compute the spreads and averages within each holding year before fitting their time-series means or alphas. This preserves the covariance between the portfolio legs in the reported standard errors.

def bivariate_returns(members, *, dependent=False):
    cells = (
        members.filter(pl.col("year") < last_holding_year)
        .group_by("year", "control", "target").agg(pl.col("excess").mean())
    )
    grid = control_grid(cells, "excess")
    control_returns = pl.col(control_ports)
    spread = grid.group_by("year").agg(
        control_returns.filter(pl.col("target") == 4).first()
        - control_returns.filter(pl.col("target") == 1).first()
    ).with_columns(target=pl.lit(5))

    rows = [grid, spread.select(grid.columns)]
    if not dependent:
        average = grid.group_by("year").agg(pl.col(control_ports).mean()).with_columns(target=pl.lit(6))
        rows.append(average.select(grid.columns))
    return (
        pl.concat(rows).sort("year", "target")
        .with_columns(Diff=pl.col("3") - pl.col("1"),
                      Avg=pl.mean_horizontal(control_ports, ignore_nulls=False))
    )

independent_returns = bivariate_returns(independent)

5.4 Independent Versus Dependent Sort
Average market capitalization makes the difference between the two methods concrete. An independent sort applies the same market-cap cutoffs across beta groups. A dependent sort can classify a stock as large among low-beta stocks even if its capitalization would place it in a lower quartile among high-beta stocks.

def average_capitalization(members):
    return (
        members.group_by("year", "control", "target").agg(pl.col("MktCap").mean())
        .group_by("control", "target").agg(pl.col("MktCap").mean())
        .pivot(on="control", index="target", values="MktCap")
        .sort("target").select("target", *control_ports)
    )

text:
6.1 Implementation
This chapter uses BEM’s annual methodology sample from Chapter 2 to illustrate the two steps of a Fama–MacBeth regression. The first step fits a cross-sectional regression in each formation year. The second averages the coefficients across years and estimates their standard errors from the time series of annual coefficients.

6.2 Interpreting FM Regressions
The ordinary Fama–MacBeth standard error is the standard deviation of the annual slopes divided by the square root of the number of years. For the size slope in the regression with all three characteristics, compare the ordinary \(t\)-statistic with the six-lag Newey–West \(t\)-statistic.

text:
7.1 The U.S. Stock Market
This chapter reconstructs the figures and tables in Chapter 7 of Bali et al. (2016). We use a later snapshot of legacy CRSP (SIZ), the same data format used by the authors. See Section 1.1.1 for source update dates.
crumbs: Part II. The Cross Section of Stock Returns
7  The CRSP Sample and Market Factor

title: 7  The CRSP Sample and Market Factor
text:
7.1.1 The CRSP U.S.-Based Common Stock Sample
At each calendar month-end, keep securities with a historical share code of 10 or 11. We do not restrict the exchange or require a price to count a stock. For market capitalization, use the absolute alternate price times shares outstanding. Dividing by 1,000 gives millions of dollars because CRSP reports shares in thousands.

import polars as pl

from era_pl import load_parquet

first = pl.date(1925, 12, 1)
last = pl.date(2012, 12, 1)

msf = (
    load_parquet("msf", "crsp")
    .with_columns(month=pl.col("date").dt.month_start())
    .filter(pl.col("month").is_between(first, last))
    .select(
        "permno", "month", "date", "altprc", "prc", "ret",
        cap=pl.when((pl.col("altprc") != 0) & (pl.col("shrout") > 0))
        .then((pl.col("altprc") * pl.col("shrout")).abs() / 1000),
    )
)

names = (
    load_parquet("msenames", "crsp")
    .filter(
        pl.col("shrcd").is_in([10, 11]),
        pl.col("namedt") <= last.dt.month_end(),
        pl.col("nameendt") >= first,
    )
    .with_columns(
        month=pl.date_ranges(
            pl.max_horizontal(pl.col("namedt").dt.month_start(), first),
            pl.min_horizontal(pl.col("nameendt").dt.month_start(), last),
            interval="1mo",
        )
    )
    .explode("month")
    .filter(pl.col("month").dt.month_end().is_between("namedt", "nameendt"))
    .select("permno", "month", "exchcd", "siccd")
)
universe = names.join(msf, on=["permno", "month"], how="left", validate="1:1")

factors = (
    load_parquet("factors_monthly", "ff")
    .select(pl.col("date").dt.month_start().alias("month"), "mktrf", "rf")
    .filter(pl.col("month").is_between(first, last))
)

cpi = (
    pl.read_csv("data/cpi-aucns.csv", try_parse_dates=True)
    .rename({"observation_date": "month", "CPIAUCNS": "cpi"})
)
if cpi.filter(pl.col("month").is_between(first, last))["month"].n_unique() != 1045:
    raise ValueError("Refresh the CPI file for December 1925–December 2012; see README.")
cpi_2012 = cpi.filter(pl.col("month") == last)["cpi"].item()



7.1.2 Composition of the CRSP Sample
Figures 7.1–7.4 of Bali et al. (2016) decompose the sample by exchange and industry from December 1925 to December 2012. Count every stock in the month-end universe, even if market capitalization is missing. For market value, sum only observed capitalization. Convert nominal millions to billions of December 2012 dollars using the ratio of December 2012 CPI to that month’s CPI.

Stock Exchange Composition of CRSP Sample
The book groups exchange codes 1 and 31 as NYSE, 2 and 32 as AMEX, and 3 and 33 as Nasdaq. All remaining codes go into Other.

from plotnine_polars import aes, guide_legend

exchange = (
    pl.when(pl.col("exchcd").is_in([1, 31])).then(pl.lit("NYSE"))
    .when(pl.col("exchcd").is_in([2, 32])).then(pl.lit("AMEX"))
    .when(pl.col("exchcd").is_in([3, 33])).then(pl.lit("Nasdaq"))
    .otherwise(pl.lit("Other"))
)

composition = (
    universe
    .filter(pl.col("month").is_between(pl.date(1925, 12, 1), pl.date(2012, 12, 1)))
    .select("month", "cap", "siccd", exchange=exchange)
    .join(cpi.lazy(), on="month", how="left", validate="m:1")
    .with_columns(real_cap=pl.col("cap") * cpi_2012 / pl.col("cpi") / 1000)
    .collect()
)

assert composition["cpi"].is_not_null().all()
assert composition["cpi"].gt(0).all()
assert composition["month"].n_unique() == 1045

def summarize_composition(sample, group, labels):
    summary = sample.group_by("month", group).agg(
        stocks=pl.len(),
        value=pl.col("real_cap").sum(),
    )
    grid = sample.select("month").unique().join(
        pl.DataFrame({group: labels}), how="cross"
    )
    return (
        grid
        .join(summary, on=["month", group], how="left", validate="1:1")
        .with_columns(pl.col("stocks", "value").fill_null(0))
        .sort("month")
    )

exchange_labels = ["NYSE", "AMEX", "Nasdaq", "Other"]
by_exchange = summarize_composition(composition, "exchange", exchange_labels)
total = (
    by_exchange
    .group_by("month")
    .agg(pl.col("stocks", "value").sum())
    .with_columns(exchange=pl.lit("Total"))
    .select(by_exchange.columns)
)
by_exchange = pl.concat([total, by_exchange])

def plot_composition(data, group, labels, measure, y_label):
    colors = [
        "#1f77b4", "#ff7f0e", "#2ca02c", "#d62728", "#9467bd", "#8c564b",
        "#e377c2", "#7f7f7f", "#bcbd22", "#17becf", "#aec7e8", "#ffbb78",
    ]
    palette = dict(zip(labels, colors))
    if "Total" in palette:
        palette["Total"] = "black"
    return (
        data.ggplot(aes(x="month", y=measure, color=group))
        .geom_line()
        .scale_x_date(date_breaks="10 years", date_labels="%Y")
        .scale_y_continuous(limits=(0, None), expand=(0, 0, 0.05, 0))
        .scale_color_manual(values=palette, breaks=labels, guide=guide_legend(ncol=3))
        .labs(x="Month", y=y_label, color="")
        .theme_minimal()
        .add_theme(figure_size=(9, 4.5), legend_position="bottom")
    )


plot_composition(by_exchange, "exchange", ["Total", *exchange_labels],
                 "stocks", "Number of stocks")







Figure 7.1: Number of stocks by exchange, recreating the series in BEM Figure 7.1.






plot_composition(by_exchange, "exchange", ["Total", *exchange_labels],
                 "value", "Market value ($ billions, December 2012)")







Figure 7.2: Market value by exchange, recreating the series in BEM Figure 7.2.





AMEX enters the data in July 1962. Most Nasdaq coverage starts in December 1972. The value series jumps much less than the count series at those dates: market coverage can change substantially without much change in market value. Keep that distinction in mind when comparing equal- and value-weighted results across time.
The December 2012 stock count includes 86 stocks in the Other category, of which 85 have no usable capitalization.1


Industry Composition of CRSP Sample
We use the security’s current SIC code rather than a code carried back from a later date. OSHA’s SIC manual describes the divisions. The table uses the intervals in BEM Table 7.1, with shortened labels. Keep zero and null codes separate from nonmissing codes that do not fall in a listed interval.

title: 7  The CRSP Sample and Market Factor
text:
7.2 Stock Returns and Excess Returns
Start with eligible common stocks at the end of month \(t\) and look up the return for the same security in month \(t+1\). Do not require it to remain in the common-stock universe in the holding month: that would screen out delistings.
Chapter 7 uses the legacy CRSP delisting return in place of the regular monthly return if the stock delists. If no delisting return is recorded, it imputes a loss of 30% for the codes listed below and a loss of 100% for other delistings. This is the book’s convention for legacy data, not a reason to adjust the reported returns from CRSP CIZ a second time.

first_return = pl.date(1926, 7, 1)
first_return_late = pl.date(1963, 7, 1)
hold_month = pl.col("month").dt.offset_by("1mo")

delist = (
    load_parquet("msedelist", "crsp")
    .with_columns(month=pl.col("dlstdt").dt.month_start())
    .filter(pl.col("month").is_between(first_return, last))
    .select("permno", "month", "dlret", "dlstcd")
)
poor_performance = (
    pl.col("dlstcd").is_in([500, 520, 580, 584])
    | pl.col("dlstcd").is_between(551, 574)
)
imputed_delist = pl.when(poor_performance).then(-0.30).otherwise(-1.00)

return_panel = (
    universe
    .with_columns(formation_month="month")
    .with_columns(month=hold_month)
    .filter(pl.col("month").is_between(first_return, last))
    .drop("ret")
    .join(
        msf.select("permno", "month", ret_raw="ret"),
        on=["permno", "month"], how="left", validate="1:1",
    )
    .join(delist, on=["permno", "month"], how="left", validate="1:1")
    .join(factors.select("month", "rf"), on="month", how="left", validate="m:1")
    .with_columns(
        ret_adj=pl.when(pl.col("dlstcd").is_not_null())
        .then(pl.coalesce("dlret", imputed_delist))
        .otherwise(pl.col("ret_raw"))
    )
    .with_columns(
        excess_raw=pl.col("ret_raw") - pl.col("rf"),
        excess_adj=pl.col("ret_adj") - pl.col("rf"),
    )
)

The Fama–French risk-free return applies to the holding month, not the formation month. We first calculate the statistics across stocks for each return month, then average those monthly statistics. In particular, the means give each month equal weight, irrespective of the number of stocks in that month. We use sample standard deviations, bias-adjusted skewness and excess kurtosis, and linearly interpolated quantiles.

def summarize_returns(start):
    x = pl.col("return_pct")
    return (
        return_panel
        .filter(pl.col("month") >= start)
        .select("month", "excess_adj", "ret_adj", "excess_raw", "ret_raw")
        .unpivot(index="month", variable_name="series", value_name="return_pct")
        .with_columns(return_pct=100 * x)
        .group_by("month", "series")
        .agg(
            n=x.count(),
            mean=x.mean(),
            sd=x.std(),
            skew=x.skew(bias=False),
            excess_kurtosis=x.kurtosis(fisher=True, bias=False),
            min=x.min(),
            p05=x.quantile(0.05, interpolation="linear"),
            p25=x.quantile(0.25, interpolation="linear"),
            median=x.median(),
            p75=x.quantile(0.75, interpolation="linear"),
            p95=x.quantile(0.95, interpolation="linear"),
            max=x.max(),
        )
        .group_by("series")
        .agg(pl.exclude("month", "series").mean())
        .collect()
    )

def display_returns(table):
    labels = {
        "excess_adj": "Adjusted excess",
        "ret_adj": "Adjusted total",
        "excess_raw": "Unadjusted excess",
        "ret_raw": "Unadjusted total",
    }
    return (
        table
        .with_columns(series=pl.col("series").replace_strict(labels))
        .unpivot(index="series", variable_name="statistic", value_name="value")
        .pivot(on="series", index="statistic", values="value")
        .select("statistic", *labels.values())
        .with_columns(pl.exclude("statistic").round(2))
    )

table_7_3 = summarize_returns(first_return_late)

7  The CRSP Sample and Market Factor

title: 7  The CRSP Sample and Market Factor
text:
7.3 The Market Factor
The Fama–French market factor (mkt) is the excess return on a broad value-weighted portfolio of U.S. common stocks. CRSP’s value-weighted market index (vwretd) has a broader set of eligible securities. We put both measures on an excess-return basis by subtracting the risk-free rate (rf) from vwretd. mkt already has the risk-free rate subtracted.

market = (
    factors
    .rename({"mktrf": "mkt"})
    .filter(pl.col("month").is_between(pl.date(1926, 7, 1), pl.date(2012, 12, 1)))
    .join(
        load_parquet("msi", "crsp")
        .select(month=pl.col("date").dt.month_start(), vwretd=pl.col("vwretd")),
        on="month", how="left", validate="1:1",
    )
    .with_columns(
        vw_excess=pl.col("vwretd") - pl.col("rf"),
        log_excess=pl.col("mkt").log1p(),
    )
    .sort("month")
    .collect()
)

The monthly correlation between mkt and the adjusted CRSP return (vw_excess) is 0.9995 in this data vintage. Following Bali et al. (2016, sec. 7.3), we summarize the monthly returns from July 1926 through December 2012. The annualized Sharpe ratio uses \(\sqrt{12}\) times the ratio of the monthly mean to the monthly standard deviation, as in the book.


series_labels = {
    "mkt": "`mkt`",
    "vw_excess": "`vwretd` less `rf`",
    "log_excess": "Log `mkt`",
}
returns = pl.col(*series_labels)
market_summary = (
    market.select(
        pl.lit(list(series_labels.values())).alias("Series"),
        pl.concat_list(returns.mean() * 100).alias("Monthly mean (%)"),
        pl.concat_list(returns.std() * 100).alias("Monthly SD (%)"),
        pl.concat_list(returns.mean() * 12**0.5 / returns.std())
        .alias("Annualized Sharpe"),
    )
    .explode(pl.all())
    .with_columns(pl.col(pl.Float64).round(3))
)

Cumulative market excess returns
For comparison with BEM Figure 7.5, we compound the monthly market factor, \(\prod_{s\leq t}(1+\mathrm{MKT}_s)-1\), and sum its log transformation, \(\sum_{s\leq t}\log(1+\mathrm{MKT}_s)\). Both are transformations of the same underlying series. The panels share a month-end date axis and use separate percentage scales.
Compounding the market factor is not the same as subtracting the compounded risk-free return from the compounded market return. Here we follow the book’s definition.

market_path = market.with_columns(
    date=pl.col("month").dt.month_end(),
    compounded=(1 + pl.col("mkt")).cum_prod() - 1,
    cumulative_log=pl.col("log_excess").cum_sum(),
)









Figure 7.5: Cumulative market excess returns, July 1926–December 2012 (compare BEM Figure 7.5).





Drawdowns
The compounded line makes early losses look small compared with later ones. To measure a drawdown, divide the value at the trough by the value at the preceding peak, then subtract one. Use the peak and trough months described in BEM; the recovery month is the first later month back at or above the old peak. Month names here refer to end-of-month values, so an episode that begins in September uses the August close as its reference.

from datetime import date

episodes = [
    ("1929 crash", date(1929, 8, 1), date(1932, 6, 1)),
    ("1968–1974 decline", date(1968, 11, 1), date(1974, 9, 1)),
    ("Dot-com bust and financial crisis", date(2000, 3, 1), date(2009, 2, 1)),
    ("1987 crash", date(1987, 8, 1), date(1987, 11, 1)),
]

wealth = market_path.select("month", wealth=1 + pl.col("compounded"))

def measure_drawdown(episode, peak, trough):
    peak_value = wealth.filter(pl.col("month") == peak)["wealth"].item()
    trough_value = wealth.filter(pl.col("month") == trough)["wealth"].item()
    recovery = wealth.filter(
        (pl.col("month") > trough) & (pl.col("wealth") >= peak_value)
    )["month"].first()
    return {
        "Episode": episode,
        "Peak": peak.strftime("%Y-%m"),
        "Trough": trough.strftime("%Y-%m"),
        "Drawdown (%)": round(100 * (trough_value / peak_value - 1), 1),
        "Recovery": recovery.strftime("%Y-%m") if recovery else "Not by 2012-12",
    }

pl.DataFrame([measure_drawdown(*episode) for episode in episodes])

title: 7  The CRSP Sample and Market Factor
text:
7.4 The CAPM Risk Model
BEM §7.4 introduces the specification rather than reporting another empirical table. To adjust a portfolio for its market exposure, regress its excess return \(r_{p,t}\) on the market excess return:
\[
r_{p,t} = \alpha_p + \beta_p\mathrm{MKT}_t + \varepsilon_{p,t}.
\]
The intercept \(\alpha_p\) is the average monthly abnormal return under this model; \(\beta_p\) is the sensitivity to the market. A portfolio long one group and short another is already a difference in returns, so subtracting the risk-free rate from both legs cancels out. Chapter 9 applies this logic and also considers the Fama–French three-factor model.

title: 8  Beta
text:
8.1 Estimating Beta
We reconstruct Tables 8.1–8.6 of Bali et al. (2016). The sample consists of CRSP common stocks at the end of each month from June 1963 through November 2012. We use legacy CRSP daily and monthly stock returns and the corresponding Fama–French factors. See Section 1.1.1 for the source vintages.
The CAPM predicts that a stock’s expected excess return is its market beta times the market risk premium, \(\mathbb E[r_i]=\beta_i\mathbb E[MKT]\). To estimate beta, regress the stock’s historical excess return \(r_{i,s}=R_{i,s}-R_{f,s}\) on the market excess return \(MKT_s\), with an intercept. For stock \(i\) at the end of month \(t\),
\[
r_{i,s}=\alpha_i+\beta_i MKT_s+\varepsilon_{i,s},
\qquad
\widehat\beta_{i,t}
=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}_{s\in W_t}(r_{i,s},MKT_s)}
{\operatorname{Var}_{s\in W_t}(MKT_s)},
\]
where \(W_t\) is the estimation window ending in month \(t\). Both moments use the same dates with valid stock and market returns. BEM use the following windows and minimum observation counts (§8.1).
Suppose a stock trades infrequently. Its return may reflect news that first moved the market on a different trading day. BEM consider two adjustments that use a year of daily returns and a 200-observation minimum. Scholes–Williams uses three separate slopes \(b_{-1}\), \(b_0\), and \(b_{+1}\) from regressing \(r_{i,s}\) on \(MKT_{s+k}\) one at a time. Dimson uses the slopes \(\gamma_k\) from one regression with all eleven market returns from \(s-5\) through \(s+5\) as predictors.
\[
\widehat\beta^{SW}_{i,t}
=\frac{\widehat b_{-1}+\widehat b_0+\widehat b_{+1}}{1+2\widehat\rho_M},
\qquad
\widehat\beta^{D}_{i,t}=\sum_{k=-5}^{5}\widehat\gamma_k,
\]
where \(\widehat\rho_M\) is the market return’s first-order autocorrelation over the estimation window. We shift the market series on the trading calendar before joining it to stock returns. A lag can precede the first stock-return date in the window. We omit response dates whose market lead falls after formation and apply the minimum to the remaining complete observations. This keeps all beta inputs observable at formation.
import polars as pl

from era_pl import load_parquet
from eap_pl import load_beta_universe, load_daily_beta_inputs

first = pl.date(1963, 6, 1)
last = pl.date(2012, 11, 1)
last_estimate = last.dt.offset_by("1mo")
keys = ["permno", "month"]

universe = load_beta_universe(first, last_estimate).collect()
We screen for common shares at formation using historical share codes 10 and 11. A stock can contribute its earlier returns to the estimation window even if its historical share code changed. We use CRSP’s reported returns for estimation and apply the delisting convention in Section 7.2 to the next-month returns used to evaluate the beta estimates.
monthly_stock = (
    load_parquet("msf", "crsp")
    .filter(pl.col("date").is_between(
        first.dt.offset_by("-59mo"), last_estimate.dt.month_end()
    ))
    .select(
        "permno",
        month=pl.col("date").dt.month_start(),
        ret=pl.col("ret").cast(pl.Float64),
        cap=pl.when((pl.col("altprc") != 0) & (pl.col("shrout") > 0))
        .then(pl.col("altprc").abs() * pl.col("shrout")),
    )
)
monthly_market = load_parquet("factors_monthly", "ff").select(
    pl.col("date").dt.month_start().alias("month"), "mktrf", "rf",
)
monthly_excess = (
    monthly_stock.join(monthly_market, on="month", validate="m:1")
    .select(*keys, "mktrf", retrf=pl.col("ret") - pl.col("rf"))
    .filter(pl.all_horizontal(pl.col("retrf", "mktrf").is_finite()))
)

def beta_slope(stock, market):
    return pl.cov(stock, market) / pl.col(market).var()
For monthly returns, we can apply the covariance-over-variance formula directly. We include the formation dates in the rolling index so a window is evaluated even if the current month’s return is missing. The window is open at its left endpoint and includes the formation month.
monthly_windows = {"1Y": (12, 10), "2Y": (24, 20), "3Y": (36, 24), "5Y": (60, 24)}
daily_windows = {"1M": (1, 15), "3M": (3, 50), "6M": (6, 100),
                 "12M": (12, 200), "24M": (24, 450)}

monthly_returns = (
    universe.lazy()
    .join(monthly_excess, on=keys, how="full", coalesce=True, validate="1:1")
    .sort(keys)
    .collect()
)

def monthly_beta(label, months, minimum):
    return (
        monthly_returns
        .rolling("month", period=f"{months}mo", group_by="permno")
        .agg(
            beta_slope("retrf", "mktrf").alias(label),
            pl.col("retrf").count().alias("n"),
        )
        .select(
            *keys,
            pl.when((pl.col("n") >= minimum) & pl.col(label).is_finite())
            .then(pl.col(label)),
        )
    )
For daily returns, each trading day enters many windows. We sum the regression inputs once per stock and month, then roll those sums across months. For example, the slope uses \(\sum xy-(\sum x)(\sum y)/n\) divided by \(\sum x^2-(\sum x)^2/n\). The adjusted regressions use the same idea with cross-products between market returns at different offsets.
daily_factors, daily_excess = load_daily_beta_inputs(
    first.dt.offset_by("-23mo"), last_estimate.dt.month_end(),
)
The tables in this chapter end with November 2012 formation, followed by December 2012 holding returns. We also estimate betas as of December 2012. The export saves all eleven estimates per stock-month to DATA_DIR/eap/betas.parquet. Chapters 9 and 10 read its 12-month daily beta for their monthly analyses. The annual methods chapters estimate their December betas when needed.

8.2 Summary Statistics
Table 8.1 averages monthly cross-sectional statistics. The count is the average number of stocks with an available estimate in a month. For example, the dispersion of the one-month daily beta reflects both differences in stocks’ exposures and estimation noise from short return histories. We use sample standard deviations, bias-adjusted skewness and excess kurtosis, and linearly interpolated quantiles.

beta_long = betas.unpivot(
    on=beta_labels, index=keys, variable_name="measure", value_name="beta",
)
b = pl.col("beta")
summary = (
    beta_long.group_by("measure", "month")
    .agg(
        mean=b.mean(), sd=b.std(), skew=b.skew(bias=False),
        kurt=b.kurtosis(fisher=True, bias=False), min=b.min(),
        p05=b.quantile(.05, interpolation="linear"),
        p25=b.quantile(.25, interpolation="linear"), median=b.median(),
        p75=b.quantile(.75, interpolation="linear"),
        p95=b.quantile(.95, interpolation="linear"), max=b.max(), n=b.count(),
    )
    .group_by("measure")
    .agg(pl.exclude("measure", "month").mean())
)

8.4 Persistence
Table 8.3 compares a stock’s winsorized beta with its beta exactly \(\tau\) calendar months later. We calculate a Pearson correlation across stocks in each month and average over months. We leave cells blank when the stock-return windows overlap. This helps distinguish persistence from the effect of using some of the same returns twice.

def persistence(lag):
    columns = [b for b in beta_labels if window_months[b] <= lag]
    current = clipped.select(*keys, *columns)
    future = current.with_columns(month=pl.col("month").dt.offset_by(f"-{lag}mo"))
    return (
        current.join(future, on=keys, suffix="_future", validate="1:1")
        .group_by("month")
        .agg(pl.corr(b, f"{b}_future").alias(b) for b in columns)
        .select(pl.lit(lag).alias("Lag (months)"), pl.col(columns).fill_nan(None).mean())
    )

persistence_table = pl.concat(
    [persistence(lag) for lag in [1, 3, 6, 12, 24, 36, 48, 60, 120]],
    how="diagonal",
)

title: 9  The Size Effect
text:
9.1 Calculating Market Capitalization
We follow Chapter 9 of Bali et al. (2016). We compare monthly and June-based size, then examine how each relates to subsequent stock returns. Formation months run from June 1963 through November 2012.
The book was published in 2016, well before CRSP’s CIZ format. This replication uses the legacy (SIZ) monthly stock and names files, not the CIZ files used in the earlier chapters. Our legacy snapshot is newer than the authors’ original data, even though we use the same sample dates. See Section 1.1.1 for the embedded update dates.
Use the share code in force at the end of each month. Keep share codes 10 and 11, without adding an exchange screen. The book’s measure uses the absolute alternate price and shares outstanding. CRSP records shares in thousands; dividing their product by 1,000 gives market capitalization in millions of dollars. Treat zeros as missing.
For the annual measure, join each stock to its capitalization at the most recent June. A stock without a record for that particular June has no annual value. We do not carry forward an older June observation.
Convert nominal market capitalization to December 2012 dollars using the BLS CPI-U, not seasonally adjusted. Use the CPI for the current observation month for both the monthly and the June-based measures, as in the book.
import polars as pl

from eap_pl import build_sizes

first = pl.date(1963, 6, 1)
last = pl.date(2012, 11, 1)
all_sizes = build_sizes()
sizes = all_sizes.filter(
    pl.col("common"), pl.col("month").is_between(first, last),
)
The table includes the earlier December market equity needed for book-to-market and December 2012 for the annual teaching sample. It records common-stock eligibility separately so the prior December price remains available when a stock’s share code changes.

prices = (
    load_parquet("msf", "crsp")
    .filter(pl.col("date").is_between(pl.date(1962, 12, 1), pl.date(2012, 12, 31)))
    .with_columns(
        month=pl.col("date").dt.month_start(),
        cap=pl.when((pl.col("altprc") != 0) & (pl.col("shrout") > 0))
        .then((pl.col("altprc") * pl.col("shrout")).abs() / 1000),
    )
    .select("permno", "month", "cap")
)
names = (
    load_parquet("msenames", "crsp")
    .select("permno", "namedt", "nameendt", "shrcd", "exchcd")
    .sort("namedt")
)
classified_months = (
    prices
    .with_columns(month_end=pl.col("month").dt.month_end())
    .sort("month_end")
    .join_asof(
        names, left_on="month_end", right_on="namedt",
        by="permno", check_sortedness=False,
    )
    .with_columns(
        common=(pl.col("month_end").is_between("namedt", "nameendt")
                & pl.col("shrcd").is_in([10, 11])).fill_null(False),
        exchcd=pl.when(pl.col("month_end").is_between("namedt", "nameendt"))
        .then(pl.col("exchcd")),
    )
    .select("permno", "month", "common", "exchcd", "cap")
)

june_caps = (
    prices
    .filter(pl.col("month").dt.month() == 6)
    .select("permno", june="month", cap_june="cap")
)
june_year = pl.col("month").dt.year() - (pl.col("month").dt.month() < 6)
stock_months = (
    classified_months
    .with_columns(june=pl.date(june_year, 6, 1))
    .join(june_caps, on=["permno", "june"], how="left", validate="m:1")
    .drop("june")
)


cpi = pl.read_csv(cpi_path, try_parse_dates=True).rename(
    {"observation_date": "month", "CPIAUCNS": "cpi"}
)
cpi_2012 = cpi.filter(pl.col("month") == pl.date(2012, 12, 1))["cpi"].item()
all_sizes = (
    stock_months
    .join(cpi.lazy(), on="month", how="left", validate="m:1")
    .with_columns(
        cap_real=pl.col("cap") * cpi_2012 / pl.col("cpi"),
        cap_june_real=pl.col("cap_june") * cpi_2012 / pl.col("cpi"),
    )
    .drop("cpi")
    .with_columns(
        pl.col("cap", "cap_real", "cap_june", "cap_june_real").log().name.prefix("log_")
    )
    .collect()
)

9.6 The Size Factor
smb is the average of three small-stock portfolios less the average of three big-stock portfolios. The three portfolios in each size group cover low, middle, and high book-to-market. Using the same book-to-market groups on both sides reduces the factor’s exposure to the value spread.
For the historical factor series we use the monthly Fama–French smb from July 1926 through December 2012.

title: 10  The Value Premium
text:
10.1 Calculating Book-to-Market Ratio
We follow Chapter 10 of Bali et al. (2016). Book-to-market compares an accounting measure of equity with what investors pay for the shares. We ask how this ratio varies across stocks and whether it predicts the following month’s excess return.
Book equity in millions is stockholders’ equity plus deferred taxes and the investment tax credit, less preferred stock. We use preferred stock redemption value, liquidation value, or par value, in that order. BEM require stockholders’ equity and deferred taxes. They use zero for a missing tax credit or when all three preferred stock fields are missing. We take the last fiscal year-end within the calendar year.
Use CRSP–Compustat links valid on the fiscal year-end. When a direct link is unavailable, try an unambiguous historical CUSIP match. We use the legacy monthly names file for this fallback.
Divide book equity by the nominal December capitalization for the same calendar year, from Chapter 9. Make that ratio available at the end of the following June and carry it through the next May. This gives a December fiscal year-end at least six months before the ratio enters a portfolio sort.
import polars as pl

from eap_pl import build_book_to_market, build_sizes

first = pl.date(1963, 6, 1)
last = pl.date(2012, 11, 1)
keys = ["permno", "month"]

all_sizes = build_sizes()
book_to_market = build_book_to_market(all_sizes)
For this chapter, use positive book equity so the logarithm is defined. The table also keeps the signed ratio for the annual summaries in Section 2.2.

funda = (
    load_parquet("funda", "comp")
    .filter(
        pl.col("indfmt") == "INDL", pl.col("datafmt") == "STD",
        pl.col("consol") == "C", pl.col("popsrc") == "D",
        pl.col("datadate").dt.year().is_between(1962, 2011),
    )
    .select(
        "gvkey", "datadate", year=pl.col("datadate").dt.year(),
        cusip=pl.col("cusip").str.slice(0, 8),
        be=pl.col("seq") + pl.col("txdb") + pl.col("itcb").fill_null(0)
        - pl.coalesce("pstkrv", "pstkl", "pstk", pl.lit(0)),
    )
    .filter(pl.col("datadate") == pl.col("datadate").max().over("gvkey", "year"))
    .unique()
    .filter(pl.len().over("gvkey", "year") == 1)
)

annual_keys = ["permno", "year"]
links = (
    load_parquet("ccmxpf_lnkused", "crsp")
    .filter(pl.col("usedflag") == 1, pl.col("ulinktype").is_in(["LU", "LC"]), pl.col("upermno") > 0)
    .select(gvkey="ugvkey", permno=pl.col("upermno").cast(pl.Int32),
            start="ulinkdt", end="ulinkenddt")
)
linked_book = (
    funda.join(links, on="gvkey")
    .filter(pl.col("datadate") >= pl.col("start"),
            (pl.col("datadate") <= pl.col("end")) | pl.col("end").is_null())
    .select("gvkey", *annual_keys, "be").unique()
)
cusips = load_parquet("msenames", "crsp").select("permno", "namedt", "nameendt", cusip="ncusip")
cusip_book = (
    funda.join(linked_book.select("gvkey", "year"), on=["gvkey", "year"], how="anti")
    .filter(pl.col("cusip").str.len_chars() == 8)
    .join(cusips, on="cusip")
    .filter(pl.col("datadate").is_between("namedt", "nameendt"))
    .select("gvkey", *annual_keys, "be").unique()
    .filter(pl.len().over("gvkey", "year") == 1)
)
book = (
    pl.concat([linked_book, cusip_book])
    .filter(pl.len().over(*annual_keys) == 1, pl.col("be").is_finite())
    .select(*annual_keys, "be")
)

december_cap = (
    sizes.lazy().filter(pl.col("month").dt.month() == 12)
    .select("permno", year=pl.col("month").dt.year(), me="cap")
)
book_to_market = (
    book.join(december_cap, on=["permno", "year"], validate="1:1")
    .with_columns(
        available=pl.date(pl.col("year") + 1, 6, 1),
        bm_raw=pl.col("be") / pl.col("me"),
    )
    .with_columns(
        month=pl.date_ranges(
            pl.col("available"), pl.col("available").dt.offset_by("11mo"),
            interval="1mo",
        ),
        bm=pl.when(pl.col("bm_raw") > 0).then(pl.col("bm_raw")),
    )
    .explode("month")
    .filter(pl.col("month") <= last.dt.offset_by("1mo"))
    .select(*keys, book_year="year", be="be", me="me", bm_raw="bm_raw",
            bm="bm", log_bm=pl.col("bm").log())
    .collect()
)

title: 10  The Value Premium
text:
10.6 The Value Factor
hml averages the high-book-to-market portfolios across the two size groups and subtracts the average of their low-book-to-market counterparts. Using small and big stocks on both sides reduces the weight of the size effect in the comparison. We use the published monthly Fama–French hml series from July 1926 through December 2012.








Figure 10.1: Cumulative returns on the Fama–French hml factor (BEM Figure 10.1)





In the Fama–French three-factor model, the intercept measures the portfolio’s return after accounting for exposures to market, size, and value factors. For excess portfolio return \(r_{p,t}\), the regression is
\[
r_{p,t}=\alpha_p+\beta_{p,M}MKT_t+\beta_{p,S}SMB_t+\beta_{p,H}HML_t+\varepsilon_{p,t}.
\]

title: 11  The Momentum Effect
text:
11.1 Measuring Momentum
Do stocks that recently outperformed continue to outperform? Following Chapter 11 of Bali et al. (2016), we compare seven measures of prior returns and examine how their predictive power changes with the return horizon. Jegadeesh and Titman (1993) document that portfolios buying recent winners and selling recent losers earn positive returns over several months.
At the end of month \(t\), the main measure compounds returns from \(t-11\) through \(t-1\). Skipping month \(t\) separates the signal from the most recent return, which is used to measure short-term reversal.
\[
\operatorname{Mom}_{i,t}
=100\left[\prod_{m=t-11}^{t-1}(1+R_{i,m})-1\right].
\tag{11.1}\]
In BEM’s Equation (11.1), \(R_{i,m}\) is the stock’s monthly return in decimal form and \(\operatorname{Mom}_{i,t}\) is measured in percentage points. We compound the available returns and require at least nine observations. For the lagged 12- and six-month alternatives, the minimum counts are ten and five. For the 12-, nine-, six-, and three-month windows that include month \(t\), the minimum counts are ten, seven, five, and three, respectively.
A calendar window counts months even when the CRSP file has a gap. The offset determines whether the window ends in month \(t\) or in month \(t-1\).
Count the nonmissing gross returns before taking their product.
import polars as pl

from eap_pl import build_book_to_market, build_momentum, build_sizes, monthly_panel

first = pl.date(1963, 6, 1)
last = pl.date(2012, 11, 1)
keys = ["permno", "month"]
signals = {
    "mom": "`mom`", "lag12": "Rₜ₋₁₂:ₜ₋₁", "lag6": "Rₜ₋₆:ₜ₋₁",
    "r12m": "`r12m`", "r9m": "`r9m`", "r6m": "`r6m`", "r3m": "`r3m`",
}

sizes = build_sizes()
book_to_market = build_book_to_market(sizes).select(*keys, "bm")
panel = (
    monthly_panel(sizes, first, last)
    .join(build_momentum(first, last), on=keys, how="left", validate="1:1")
    .join(book_to_market, on=keys, how="left", validate="1:1")
)
The formation sample runs from June 1963 through November 2012. The panel uses the beta, size, and positive book-to-market measures from Chapter 8, Chapter 9, and Chapter 10. Holding-month excess returns use the delisting treatment in Section 7.2.

def _compound_trailing_return(returns, name, length, skip, minimum):
    gross = pl.col("gross")
    return returns.rolling(
        "month", period=f"{length}mo", offset=f"-{length + skip}mo",
        group_by="permno", closed="right",
    ).agg(
        pl.when(gross.count() >= minimum).then(100 * (gross.product() - 1)).alias(name)
    )

text:
11.4 Momentum and Stock Returns

11.4.1 Univariate Portfolio Analysis
Each month, sort the stocks with a valid signal into ten portfolios using breakpoints from all stocks with that signal. Value weights use market capitalization at formation. Returns and alphas are in percentage points per month. For each winner-minus-loser spread, regress the monthly return series on an intercept, on the market factor, or on the three Fama–French factors to estimate its mean, CAPM alpha, or FF alpha. Parentheses report six-lag Newey–West \(t\)-statistics (Newey and West 1987).

from era_pl import load_parquet
from eap_pl import format_fit, hac
from eap_pl._portfolios import assign_portfolio, portfolio_months, spread

factors = (
    load_parquet("factors_monthly", "ff")
    .select(
        month=pl.col("date").dt.month_start(),
        market=100 * pl.col("mktrf"),
        smb=100 * pl.col("smb"),
        hml=100 * pl.col("hml"),
        rf=100 * pl.col("rf"),
    )
    .collect()
)
ff3 = ["market", "smb", "hml"]
weights = {"VW": "Value weighted", "EW": "Equal weighted"}


def spread_statistics(series, weight, *, ff_factors=ff3, capm=True):
    sample = (series.select("month", weight)
              .join(factors, on="month", validate="m:1").sort("month"))
    models = {"Return": "1"}
    if capm:
        models["CAPM α"] = "market"
    models["FF α"] = " + ".join(ff_factors)
    return {
        name: format_fit(hac(f"{weight} ~ {rhs}", sample), "Intercept")
        for name, rhs in models.items()
    }


deciles = {str(i): i for i in range(1, 11)}
formation = panel.select(*keys, "cap", *signals)
members = {
    signal: assign_portfolio(
        formation.select(*keys, "cap", signal).filter(pl.col(signal).is_finite()),
        signal, 10, "month",
    ).drop(signal)
    for signal in signals
}

one_month = panel.select(*keys, "market", "excess")
decile_returns = {
    signal: portfolio_months(
        stocks.join(one_month, on=keys, validate="1:1")
        .with_columns(pl.col("month").dt.offset_by("1mo")),
        ["portfolio"],
    )

11.4.2 Returns at Longer Horizons
Keep the formation-month decile assignments and capitalization weights. For each \(k\), attach the return in month \(t+k\) and compute the spread across stocks with a return in that month. A delisting contributes its adjusted return in the month it occurs. We use realized returns through December 2012 and match the factors to the month in which each return is realized.

from eap_pl._data import monthly_stock_returns

holding_returns = (
    monthly_stock_returns(first.dt.offset_by("1mo"), last.dt.offset_by("1mo"))
    .collect()
    .join(factors.select("month", "rf", "market"), on="month", validate="m:1")
    .select("permno", "market", holding="month", excess=100 * pl.col("ret") - pl.col("rf"))
)


def returns_at_horizon(stocks, k):
    realized = (
        stocks.with_columns(holding=pl.col("month").dt.offset_by(f"{k}mo"))
        .drop("month")
        .join(holding_returns, on=["permno", "holding"], validate="1:1")
        .rename({"holding": "month"})
    )
    return portfolio_months(realized, ["portfolio"])

11.4.3 Controlling for Market Capitalization
First divide stocks into five capitalization groups. Then compute mom quintile breakpoints separately within each capitalization group. The last column averages the control portfolios each month before calculating the mean return or estimating an alpha.

from eap_pl import bivariate_months

sort_panel = panel.select(*keys, "mom", "beta", "cap", "bm", "excess", "market")


def two_way_results(
    monthly, weight, control_labels, *, ff_factors=ff3, show_cells=False, show_average=True,
):
    groups = monthly.partition_by("control", as_dict=True)
    series = {label: groups[i,] for i, label in enumerate(control_labels, 1)}
    if show_average:
        series["Average"] = monthly.group_by("month", "target").agg(
            pl.col(weight).mean(), pl.col("market").first(),
        )

    rows = []
    if show_cells:
        for target in range(1, 6):
            rows.append({
                "Statistic": f"`mom` {target}",
                **{label: f'{cell.filter(pl.col("target") == target)[weight].mean():.2f}'
                   for label, cell in series.items()},
            })

    stats = {
        label: spread_statistics(
            spread(cell, 5, 1, "target", weight).with_columns(
                pl.col("month").dt.offset_by("1mo")
            ),
            weight, ff_factors=ff_factors,
        )
        for label, cell in series.items()
    }
    rows.extend({
        "Statistic": f"5–1 {metric}",
        **{label: value[metric] for label, value in stats.items()},
    } for metric in ("Return", "CAPM α", "FF α"))
    return [{"Weights": weights[weight], **row} for row in rows]


quintiles = [str(i) for i in range(1, 6)]

11.4.5 Controlling for Beta and Book-to-Market
The dependent sorts calculate mom breakpoints within each beta or bm quintile. The independent sorts use the intersection of two sets of breakpoints computed separately across stocks for each variable. The tables show the high-minus-low mom spread within each control quintile and its average across the control quintiles.

sort_variables = {"beta": "Beta", "cap": "Market cap", "bm": "`bm`"}


def two_way_spreads(pairs, *, dependent, momentum_first=False):
    rows = []
    for control, target in pairs:
        monthly = bivariate_months(sort_panel, control, target, nyse=False, dependent=dependent)
        omit = {"cap": "smb", "bm": "hml"}.get(target)
        ff_factors = [factor for factor in ff3 if factor != omit]
        characteristic = target if momentum_first else control
        for weight in weights:
            rows.extend(
                {"Characteristic": sort_variables[characteristic], **row}
                for row in two_way_results(monthly, weight, quintiles, ff_factors=ff_factors)
            )
    return pl.DataFrame(rows)

title: 11  The Momentum Effect
text:
11.5 The Momentum Factor
The Kenneth French Data Library constructs its momentum factor using six value-weighted portfolios formed on size and prior return. The sorts use an NYSE median for size and NYSE 30th and 70th percentiles for prior return. The factor averages the returns of the small- and large-stock winner portfolios and subtracts the average return of the corresponding loser portfolios. We use the December 2024 release listed in the book’s setup instructions and plot January 1927 through December 2012, the period in BEM.

from io import StringIO
from pathlib import Path
import re

from eap_pl import plot_cumulative_returns

archive = Path("data/momentum-202412.csv").read_text()
monthly_rows = re.findall(r"(?m)^\s*(\d{6},[^\r\n]+)", archive)
momentum_factor = (
    pl.read_csv(
        StringIO("\n".join(monthly_rows)), has_header=False, new_columns=["ym", "mom"],
        schema_overrides={"mom": pl.String},
    )
    .filter(pl.col("ym").is_between(192701, 201212))
    .select(
        date=(pl.col("ym").cast(pl.String) + "01").str.to_date("%Y%m%d"),
        mom=pl.col("mom").str.strip_chars().cast(pl.Float64) / 100,
    )
    .sort("date")
    .with_columns(
        compounded=(1 + pl.col("mom")).cum_prod() - 1,
        cumulative_log=pl.col("mom").log1p().cum_sum(),
    )
)
assert momentum_factor.height == 1032
assert momentum_factor.select(pl.col("mom").is_finite().all()).item()
plot_cumulative_returns(momentum_factor, y_label="Cumulative momentum factor return")







Figure 11.1: Compounded and cumulative log returns of the momentum factor, January 1927–December 2012 (BEM Figure 11.1)





The compounded series shows a sharp drawdown in 2009.

title: 11  The Momentum Effect
text:
11.6 The Fama–French–Carhart Four-Factor Model
Carhart (1997) adds a momentum factor to the three stock-market factors of Fama and French (1993). The four-factor model is BEM’s Equation (11.2).
\[
r_{p,t}=\alpha_p+\beta_{\mathrm{MKT},p}\mathrm{MKT}_t
+\beta_{\mathrm{SMB},p}\mathrm{SMB}_t+\beta_{\mathrm{HML},p}\mathrm{HML}_t
+\beta_{\mathrm{MOM},p}\mathrm{MOM}_t+\varepsilon_{p,t}.
\tag{11.2}\]
Here \(r_{p,t}\) is the excess return of portfolio \(p\), and \(\alpha_p\) is the intercept after accounting for its exposures to the market, size, value, and momentum factors.




Bali, Turan G., Robert F. Engle, and Scott Murray. 2016. Empirical Asset Pricing: The Cross Section of Stock Returns. John Wiley & Sons. https://www.wiley.com/en-us/empirical-asset-pricing-the-cross-section-of-stock-returns-p-9781118095041.


Carhart, Mark M. 1997. “On Persistence in Mutual Fund Performance.” The Journal of Finance 52 (1): 57–82. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.1997.tb03808.x.


Fama, Eugene F., and Kenneth R. French. 1993. “Common Risk Factors in the Returns on Stocks and Bonds.” Journal of Financial Economics 33 (1): 3–56. https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-405X(93)90023-5.


Jegadeesh, Narasimhan, and Sheridan Titman. 1993. “Returns to Buying Winners and Selling Losers: Implications for Stock Market Efficiency.” The Journal of Finance 48 (1): 65–91. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.1993.tb04702.x.


Newey, Whitney K., and Kenneth D. West. 1987. “A Simple, Positive Semi-Definite, Heteroskedasticity and Autocorrelation Consistent Covariance Matrix.” Econometrica 55 (3): 703–8. https://doi.org/10.2307/1913610.

title: 12  Short-Term Reversal
text:
12.1 Measuring Short-Term Reversal
Do stocks that rose last month continue to outperform, or do they give back some of their gains? Following Chapter 12 of Bali et al. (2016), we sort on the most recent monthly return and compare its predictive power with that of earlier returns. This complements Chapter 11, where the main momentum signal skips the formation month.
In BEM’s Equation (12.1), the reversal signal is the formation-month CRSP stock return in percentage points.
\[
\operatorname{Rev}_{i,t}=100 R_{i,t}.
\tag{12.1}\]
Here \(R_{i,t}\) is the decimal return for stock \(i\) in month \(t\). Earlier returns are also expressed in percentage points and matched by calendar month, so a gap in the CRSP file does not make an older observation count as the previous month’s return. The formation sample runs from June 1963 through November 2012, and the outcome is the following month’s excess return, including the delisting treatment in Section 7.2.
import polars as pl

from era_pl import load_parquet
from eap_pl import build_book_to_market, build_momentum, build_sizes, monthly_panel

first = pl.date(1963, 6, 1)
last = pl.date(2012, 11, 1)
keys = ["permno", "month"]
lag_labels = {"rev": "`rev`", **{f"lag{k}": f"R(t−{k})" for k in range(1, 12)}}
stock_returns = (
    load_parquet("msf", "crsp")
    .filter(pl.col("date").is_between(first.dt.offset_by("-11mo"), last.dt.month_end()))
    .select(
        "permno", month=pl.col("date").dt.month_start(),
        rev=pl.when(pl.col("ret").is_finite()).then(100 * pl.col("ret")),
    )
)

sizes = build_sizes()
book_to_market = build_book_to_market(sizes).select(*keys, "bm")
panel = (
    monthly_panel(sizes, first, last).lazy()
    .join(book_to_market.lazy(), on=keys, how="left", validate="1:1")
    .join(build_momentum(first, last).select(*keys, "mom").lazy(),
          on=keys, how="left", validate="1:1")
    .join(stock_returns, on=keys, how="left", validate="1:1")
)
for k in range(1, 12):
    lagged = stock_returns.select(
        "permno", month=pl.col("month").dt.offset_by(f"{k}mo"), **{f"lag{k}": pl.col("rev")},
    ).filter(pl.col("month").is_between(first, last))
    panel = panel.join(lagged, on=keys, how="left", validate="1:1")

title: 12  Short-Term Reversal
text:
12.5 The Short-Term Reversal Factor
The Kenneth French short-term reversal factor uses six value-weighted portfolios formed by intersecting two size groups and three prior-return groups. The cutoffs are the NYSE median capitalization and the NYSE 30th and 70th percentiles of the previous month’s return. The factor buys recent losers and sells recent winners, so its sign is opposite to the high-minus-low spreads above.
\[
\mathrm{STR}_{t+1}
=\frac{R_{\mathrm{Small,Low},t+1}+R_{\mathrm{Big,Low},t+1}}{2}
-\frac{R_{\mathrm{Small,High},t+1}+R_{\mathrm{Big,High},t+1}}{2}.
\tag{12.2}\]
We use the French library’s December 2024 archive and plot the same July 1926–December 2012 window as BEM. With \(\mathrm{STR}_m\) in decimal units, the two panels use the following scales.
\[
C_t=\prod_{m\le t}(1+\mathrm{STR}_m)-1,
\qquad
L_t=\sum_{m\le t}\log(1+\mathrm{STR}_m).
\tag{12.3}\]

from eap_pl import plot_cumulative_returns

reversal_factor = (
    archived_factor("data/st-reversal-202412.csv", "str")
    .filter(pl.col("month").is_between(pl.date(1926, 7, 1), pl.date(2012, 12, 1)))
    .rename({"month": "date"})
    .sort("date")
    .with_columns(pl.col("str") / 100)
    .with_columns(
        compounded=(1 + pl.col("str")).cum_prod() - 1,
        cumulative_log=pl.col("str").log1p().cum_sum(),
    )
)
assert reversal_factor["date"].equals(
    pl.date_range(pl.date(1926, 7, 1), pl.date(2012, 12, 1), "1mo", eager=True)
)
assert reversal_factor.select(pl.col("str").is_finite().fill_null(False).all()).item()
plot_cumulative_returns(reversal_factor, y_label="Cumulative reversal factor return")







Figure 12.1: Compounded and cumulative log returns of the short-term reversal factor (BEM Figure 12.1)





The archived series compounds to 121,099% and reaches a cumulative log return of 710.00%.
To estimate the four-factor alpha, use January 1927 through December 2012 because the momentum factor starts in January 1927. The regression outcome is in percentage points per month.

str_sample = (
    reversal_factor.select(month="date", str_pct=100 * pl.col("str"))
    .join(factors.drop_nulls("mom_factor"), on="month", validate="1:1")
    .sort("month")
)
str_fit = hac("str_pct ~ mkt + smb + hml + mom_factor", str_sample)

The four-factor alpha is 0.78% per month (\(t\) = 6.10).




Bali, Turan G., Robert F. Engle, and Scott Murray. 2016. Empirical Asset Pricing: The Cross Section of Stock Returns. John Wiley & Sons. https://www.wiley.com/en-us/empirical-asset-pricing-the-cross-section-of-stock-returns-p-9781118095041.
